description: We are a community team with three middle school students and one high school student. Some of our skills and interests are CAD design, software, AI usage, gaming, video creation, writing, and much more.
summary: We developed a game that helps young children to have fun playing it, while encountering real NASA data and learning how to run a Martian Outpost. It's important, because most learning games that exist right now oversimplify things or are too complex/too boring for young kids. Our game has elementary school students juggle between managing supplies and fighting aliens coming to attack our outpost.
details:
Outpost: Mars

What it does

A spaceship headed towards Mars breaks upon landing, with only three days of food, water, air, and power left. Players need to manage 6 parameters (power, food, water, air, health, and shield defense) to keep the outpost running. All resources drain over time, and you need to decide how to replenish these things while rebuilding your rocket. Every action costs something, so you need to make real mission-planning decisions. Outpost: Mars teaches young children how life support, power, radiation, space weather, and much more can affect an outpost success while incorporating real NASA data and space facts into it.

How it works

  • Survival: Each Mars day lasts two real minutes (one minute of daylight, one of night). Water, food, air and shield replenishment buttons convert power into supplies. Power can be earned through pedaling, burning biofuel, solar panels, and nuclear power.
  • Upgrades: Upgrade trees cover power, weapons (blasters, lasers, EMP, plasma cannon), shield (wall dome, electro shield, gravity shield), and water, food and air systems. Each ends with a more efficient machine that gains you more resources.
  • Defend: From day 6, seven alien types attack: Skitter, Swooper, Splatter, Marauder, Spitter, Crusher and Overlord. Players can tap aliens to zap them, and the aliens drop supplies needed to get upgrades and build rocket parts.
  • Real space weather: NASA DONKI records from January 2016 are used to create the solar flares and sun shock waves in Outpost: Mars. Each game day matches the corresponding day in January, and the month repeats after day 30. Each event shows the real date and magnitude of the natural disasters, such as the M2.3 flare recorded on January 1, 2016. Players choose how to respond (for example, shelter the crew or keep working), but both options will cost you something.
  • Other hazards: Dust storms, fires, marsquakes, and meteor showers add pressure.
  • Mines and workshop: Drills dig metal and minerals, and the inventory workshop can turn them into steel.
  • Learn: 22 quests send explorers out and each ends with a question about Martian facts. Topics include the Olympus Mons, dust devils and why Mars is red. The first 12 give a 5% defense bonus. Random pop quizzes also help players by awarding them free supplies.
  • Win or lose: Build all five rocket parts (hull, engines, fuel tank, navigation, crew pod) and launch towards Earth to win. The game is lost if the crew's life bar reaches zero, where Captain Nova evacuates everyone back to Earth for a gentler ending.
  • Guidance: Captain Nova leads a guided tutorial, and an intro movie sets up the story. The game has read-aloud narration, music, a save code to continue later, and a game-over escape scene.

Benefits and impact

  • Shows how mission design trades off power, life support, defense and time, with every choice costing something.
  • Turns real NASA space weather data into game events, so players see why radiation and solar activity matter on Mars.
  • Teaches Mars facts and space science through quests, quizzes and fun facts, with text-to-speech to help younger readers.

NASA data and resources used

  • NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information): January 2016 solar flare and interplanetary shock records.
  • NASA mission facts used in the game: MOXIE and Perseverance, InSight marsquakes, Valles Marineris, Olympus Mons.

Tools and technologies

From the code, the game is a single HTML file built with JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas for the pixel-art scene and effects, the Web Audio API for sound effects and music, browser local storage for save codes, and Google Fonts. It is hosted on GitHub Pages. We used Claude Ai to help us create the visuals and code for the game, and ElevenLabs for the audio in game.
